1.pericope_label: The LORD challenges Job again, shall he that contendeth with the Almighty instruct him; Job answers that he is vile and will speak no more

schools.summary: Gill reads the opening as a resumption after a deliberate pause, asks whether a man can instruct the God who gives men wisdom and answers that the man who submits may be instructed while the man who contends is not in the way of instruction at all, and offers four senses of Job calling himself vile, his arguments shown powerless, his integrity found wanting, his distance from God as dust and ashes, or the vileness of his nature newly seen.

Henry has God clench the nail with one demand more after heaping up hard questions, notes that the speech is not said to come from the whirlwind so that some take it for a still small voice, and hears disdain in the question, since it asks whether God shall take instruction from every peevish complainer and change his settled measures to please him.

Clarke shows from the word that answered refers to nothing Job had said, argues at length that these fourteen verses were originally the ending of the poem and gives the reader the rearrangement to try, and takes the confession for an acknowledgement of inward defilement by a man confounded at the high thoughts he had entertained of his righteousness.

Ellicott prefers a different construction of the question and glosses it as asking whether Job will keep disputing and whether there is hope of convincing God by argument; he knows the transposition proposal and declines it as unnecessary and unsupported by external evidence. Delitzsch makes the term for the man a fault-finder and draws the moral from God manner, that he demands free submission rather than blind subjection and effects the acknowledgement by persuasion.

debates.question: Should the first fourteen verses be transposed to the end of the poem?

sides.position: very likely yes: the former part of the chapter is evidently the conclusion, the latter part is in disorder, the parchment skins of the roll having probably changed places, and the last chapter shows Jehovah speaks last
the transposition would make these verses the climax and remove the awkwardness of Job speaking after resolving not to, but it is unnecessary and has no support from external evidence

debates.question: What does the question about instructing the Almighty ask?

sides.position: whether a man is capable of instructing the God of knowledge at all; the contender is not in the way of instruction, the word carrying the sense of chastisement
whether Job is prepared to go on disputing, and whether there is any hope of convincing God in argument
whether Job will persist; the fault-finder who sets God right must answer the questions put to him
it is a question of disdain: shall God take instruction from every peevish complainer and change his measures to please him

debates.question: Why does God answer a man who has said nothing?

sides.position: because he knows men thoughts and can return a suitable answer to their silence
because answered refers to no question asked, but means that the Lord continued his discourse
because God paused for Job to speak and, finding him silent, began again

outliers: Henry alone suggests the second challenge may have come in a still small voice rather than the whirlwind, as to Elijah.
Delitzsch alone turns the scene against the friends, those sticklers for their own orthodoxy, as proof that God is more forbearing than men.
themes: a silence that is itself answered
a complainer who would teach God his business
a poem whose ending may have been displaced
a confession not yet deep enough

6.pericope_label: Out of the whirlwind again: hast thou an arm like God, deck thyself with majesty, abase the proud, and then I will confess thy right hand can save thee

schools.summary: Gill holds that the whirlwind grew more boisterous rather than ceasing, since it was not enough for Job to call himself vile and God would have a fuller confession; he takes disannulling the judgment for setting one own judgment against the Lord decrees, has Job told to put on the airs of a wrathful king to see whether that humbles a proud man, and offers three senses of hiding the proud in the dust.

Henry lays down that those who profit by what they have heard shall hear more and that the truly penitent still need deeper penitence, warning the convicted not to catch at comfort too soon since the wound must be searched to the bottom and not skinned over, and works the comparison item by item, man being unable to speak with the force of a God who speaks and it is done.

Clarke suspects the renewed challenge was repeated from the earlier speech by later hands joining a wrong gathering of parchment, hears in the charge a willingness to condemn God conduct sooner than be thought in the wrong, reads the binding of the faces as the custom of preserving mummies, and turns the closing irony into the doctrine that salvation belongs to God alone.

Ellicott supplies the argument that holds the challenge together, that Job inability to govern the formidable animals proves his inability to govern the world morally, so that he can neither tread down the wicked nor deliver himself from the hand of God. Delitzsch finds the climax over the first question, Job having gone so far as to doubt the divine justice rather than surrender his own righteousness, and makes the commands a robing of the subject in the robes of the King of kings.

debates.question: Why does God speak a second time?

sides.position: because Job was humbled but not enough; a fuller confession was wanted, of sorrow and repentance and of having spoken what he did not understand
because those truly convinced of sin still need to be made more deeply penitent, and must not catch at comfort too soon
because this verse and the next were repeated here from the earlier speech by later hands joining a wrong gathering of the parchment

debates.question: What is the force of disannulling God judgment?

sides.position: setting a man own judgment against the Lord decrees, sentence or execution, none of which can be hindered
condemning God conduct rather than be thought in the wrong, a sort of blasphemy men back into
losing sight of the divine justice in the government of the world, and doubting it rather than surrender his own righteousness

debates.question: How do the impossible commands work?

sides.position: as irony that tests whether such means can humble a proud man
as a robing of the subject in the robes of the King of kings, to send wrath over pride for its complete removal
as a comparison man cannot sustain, since one of God thunders would overrule all our whispers

outliers: Clarke alone reads the binding of the faces in secret as the swathing of mummies under rollers never meant to be removed.
Clarke alone observes that there are three words hardest of all to pronounce in any language.
Ellicott alone builds the bridge from the brute creation to the moral government of the world.
themes: a storm that does not abate at the first confession
an arm measured against the arm of God
majesty offered to a man to wear
salvation conceded only to one right hand

15.pericope_label: Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee: his strength, his bones like bars of iron, and he the chief of the ways of God

schools.summary: Gill starts from the received identification with the elephant but will not hold it, reporting the dissent for the river horse and weighing the clauses against the elephant one by one, the strength in the loins agreeing badly, the bones porous rather than iron, and the tail suiting the river horse better; on the chief of the ways of God he allows either the beginning of God works, which would set the river horse a day before the elephant, or a superiority limited to its own kind.

Henry sees no reason to leave the received opinion that the elephant is meant, a creature of larger stature than any other and too celebrated to be left out of a survey of four-footed beasts, and frames the description as a question whether a man can contend with him who made the beast and gave him his power.

Clarke shows that neither the name nor the ancient versions settle the identification, allows that the balance of characters lies with the hippopotamus, but doubts whether any animal now in existence is the one described and supposes with Good that it is extinct, pointing to three lost genera whose skeletons have been recovered.

Ellicott takes the plural seriously and suggests more than one animal may be meant, the first verses answering to the elephant and the last to the hippopotamus, states the objection to his own suggestion, offers a Coptic word meaning water-ox as concealed in the name, and corrects three renderings in as many verses. Delitzsch leaves the identification and settles the form, the plural carrying no numerical force but denoting the beast as such.

sides.position: the elephant, on the ancient and generally received opinion
rather the river horse, since the strength in the loins, the iron bones and the tail all agree with it better than with the elephant
neither; the balance of characters favours the hippopotamus, but parts of the description suit no living animal, and the creature is probably extinct
possibly more than one animal, the earlier verses describing the elephant and the later the hippopotamus
the question of species is left aside; the plural form denotes the beast as such, the giant among beasts

debates.question: In what sense is he the chief of the ways of God?

sides.position: either as the beginning of God works among the animals, or as a superiority limited to his own kind, since man is chief of all God works
the title fits the elephant better, for its intelligence and usefulness

outliers: Clarke alone appeals to the recovered skeletons of three lost genera, one of which he had examined himself.
Ellicott alone finds in the plural form of the name a reason to suspect that two animals are described.
Gill alone collects the testimonies that hippopotamus teeth are valued above ivory and harder to work.
themes: a beast named in the plural
characters that fit no living animal
a creature made alongside the man addressed

20.pericope_label: The mountains bring him forth food; he lies under the shady trees and drinks up a river, and is taken only by craft

schools.summary: Gill lets the mountain pasture tell against neither candidate, marvels that a beast bred in a river should feed on a mountain and supports the possibility from the northern sea morss, finds the shade fitting the river horse since the elephant is said to sleep standing, thinks drinking up a river too great an hyperbole and prefers the rendering that he neither hurries nor is frightened though the river press on him, and reads the taking as a question answered by the covered pit.

Clarke takes the mountain pasture to rule out the hippopotamus, declines to decide on the lying down since these habits are unknown to us, infers from the naming of Jordan that the creature once inhabited the mountains and marshes of Palestine, and closes by committing himself to the mastodon or mammoth, made as the chief of God works, exhibited for a time and then cut off with its skeletons preserved.

Ellicott judges the shade more appropriate to the elephant and cautions that the critics judgment has been biased by assumptions about where the book was written, and renders the river clause as his being confident though Jordan swell up to his mouth. Delitzsch leaves the animal and identifies the tree as the wild lote, found in Syria and Egypt and through Africa, citing the poets for the beasts of the steppe that seek its shade.

debates.question: Does the mountain pasture settle the identification?

sides.position: yes, against the hippopotamus, which is seldom found far from its rivers; the description answers to the mammoth
no, since grass grows on mountains and feeds the river horse as well, though it is a marvel that a river beast should feed there

debates.question: Whom does the lying down under the shade suit?

sides.position: the elephant, on the whole, if the description applies to one animal at all
the river horse, since the elephant is reported to sleep standing and to be taller than the trees
undecidable, these being habits with which we are and must be unacquainted

debates.question: How should the drinking of the river be read?

sides.position: not as hyperbole but as composure: though a river press on him with all its force he neither hurries out nor is frightened
as a figure of unstoppable course, no river staying him, with Jordan named because he once inhabited Palestine

outliers: Gill alone brings in the northern sea morss, which climbs from the sea to the mountain tops by its teeth.
Ellicott alone accuses the critics of letting their view of where the book was written decide the identification.
Delitzsch alone abandons the zoology for the botany of the shade tree.
themes: a river beast pastured on a mountain
a creature unmoved by a flood
an identification left open on purpose
